items.prompt: What part of the body is the main place where taste buds are found?

options.label: The tongue
options.feedback: Correct. Most taste buds sit on the tongue, though a few are also found on the roof, sides and back of the mouth, and in the throat.

options.label: The lips
options.feedback: The lips have no taste buds. Taste buds are located on the tongue and in parts of the mouth and throat, not on the lips.

options.label: The teeth
options.feedback: Teeth are hard structures for chewing, not for sensing taste. Taste buds are soft clusters of cells on the tongue and elsewhere in the mouth.

options.label: The nose
options.feedback: The nose is for smell, not taste. Taste buds are found in the mouth, mainly on the tongue.

items.ok_line: The tongue holds most of the taste buds.
items.ko_line: Taste buds live in the mouth, not on lips, teeth, or nose.
items.exp_text: Taste buds are clusters of receptor cells found mostly on the tongue, with a smaller number on the roof, sides and back of the mouth, and in the throat.

items.prompt: What are the small bumps visible on the tongue's surface called?

options.label: Taste buds
options.feedback: Those bumps are not the taste buds themselves. Each bump, called a papilla, contains hundreds of taste buds inside it.

options.label: Papillae
options.feedback: Correct. The tongue is covered with thousands of small bumps called papillae, and inside most of them sit the taste buds.

options.label: Receptor cells
options.feedback: Receptor cells are the individual cells inside a taste bud, not the visible bumps on the tongue. The bumps are the papillae.

options.label: Olfactory epithelium
options.feedback: That is the tissue in the nose that detects smell, not the bumps on the tongue. The tongue's bumps are papillae.

items.ko_line: The bumps are papillae, and the buds are inside them.
items.exp_text: Papillae are the small bumps you can see on the tongue. Most of them contain hundreds of taste buds, which are too small to see with the naked eye.

items.prompt: How many basic tastes can the taste receptors in the mouth sense?

options.label: Four
options.feedback: Four was once believed, but scientists now recognise a fifth. The full set includes sweetness, sourness, saltiness, bitterness, and savoriness.

options.label: Three
options.feedback: There are more than three. The five basic tastes are sweetness, sourness, saltiness, bitterness, and savoriness.

options.label: Six
options.feedback: Pungency was once suggested as a sixth, but it is not counted among the five basic tastes. The recognised set has exactly five.

options.label: Five
options.feedback: Correct. The five basic tastes are sweetness, sourness, saltiness, bitterness, and savoriness (umami).

items.ko_line: The recognised number is five, not four, three, or six.
items.exp_text: Taste receptors detect five distinct basic tastes: sweetness, sourness, saltiness, bitterness, and savoriness, also called umami.

items.prompt: Which taste warns people of poisons in food?

options.label: Sweetness
options.feedback: Sweetness signals energy-rich foods, which the body craves. It does not warn of poisons; bitterness does.

options.label: Saltiness
options.feedback: Saltiness helps the body keep its water and ion balance, not warn of poisons. Bitterness is the warning taste.

options.label: Bitterness
options.feedback: Correct. Bitterness serves as a warning that something may be poisonous, so it often triggers caution.

options.label: Savoriness
options.feedback: Savoriness signals the presence of amino acids and proteins, which are needed and pleasurable. It does not warn of poisons.

items.ko_line: It is bitterness, not sweet, salty, or savoury.
items.exp_text: Bitterness is the taste that alerts people to possible poisons, while sweetness and savoriness attract them to useful food.

items.prompt: What does sweetness in food mostly signal the presence of?

options.label: Carbohydrates
options.feedback: Correct. Sweetness signals carbohydrates in solution, which provide the body with a rich source of energy.

options.label: Proteins
options.feedback: Proteins are signalled by savoriness, not sweetness. Sweetness points to carbohydrates.

options.label: Acids
options.feedback: Acids are detected as sour, not sweet. Sweetness points to carbohydrates.

options.label: Salts
options.feedback: Salts are detected as salty, not sweet. Sweetness points to carbohydrates.

items.ko_line: Sweetness is about carbohydrates, not proteins, acids, or salts.
items.exp_text: Sweet taste indicates the presence of carbohydrates, which the body uses for direct energy and storage, so it is usually a pleasant sensation.

items.prompt: Which taste signals the presence of the amino acid L-glutamate?

options.label: Sourness
options.feedback: Sourness is the taste of acids, not amino acids. The taste that signals L-glutamate is savoriness.

options.label: Savoriness
options.feedback: Correct. Savoriness, known in Japanese as umami, signals the presence of the amino acid L-glutamate.

options.label: Bitterness
options.feedback: Bitterness warns of poisons. The taste that signals L-glutamate is savoriness.

options.label: Saltiness
options.feedback: Saltiness signals ions, particularly sodium chloride. The taste that signals L-glutamate is savoriness.

items.ko_line: It is savoriness, not sour, bitter, or salty.
items.exp_text: The savory taste, also called umami, signals the presence of the amino acid L-glutamate, which the body uses to build proteins.

items.prompt: Which of these tastes does a cat not have the ability to sense?

options.label: Sweetness
options.feedback: Correct. Cats cannot taste sweetness, which is one of the basic tastes they have lost.

options.label: Saltiness
options.feedback: Cats can still taste saltiness. The taste they have lost is sweetness.

options.label: Sourness
options.feedback: Cats can still taste sourness. The taste they have lost is sweetness.

options.label: Bitterness
options.feedback: Cats can still taste bitterness. The taste they have lost is sweetness.

items.ko_line: It is sweetness that cats lack, not salt, sour, or bitter.
items.exp_text: Not all mammals share the same tastes: cats specifically cannot taste sweetness, while some other carnivores have lost up to four of the five basic tastes.

items.prompt: What happens to the sense of taste as humans age?

options.label: It becomes sharper
options.feedback: Taste does not sharpen with age; it actually begins to fade. The papillae are lost and saliva production slows down.

options.label: It stays exactly the same
options.feedback: Taste changes with age in humans: it fades, papillae are lost, and saliva production decreases.

options.label: It begins to fade
options.feedback: Correct. Among humans, taste perception begins to fade during ageing, along with a loss of tongue papillae and slower saliva production.

options.label: It only affects bitter tastes
options.feedback: Ageing affects the overall sense of taste, not just one taste. Perception fades generally, and papillae are lost.

items.ko_line: Ageing worsens taste, not sharpens or preserves it.
items.exp_text: With ageing, taste perception fades, papillae on the tongue are lost, and saliva production decreases, so food may taste less strong.

items.prompt: Where are taste buds located besides the tongue?

options.label: Only in the nose
options.feedback: The nose is for smell, not taste. Besides the tongue, taste buds are in the mouth and throat.

options.label: Only on the lips
options.feedback: Lips have no taste buds. Taste buds are found on the roof, sides and back of the mouth, and in the throat.

options.label: Only in the stomach
options.feedback: The stomach digests food; it does not house taste buds. They are in the mouth and throat, not the stomach.

options.label: In the mouth and throat
options.feedback: Correct. Besides the tongue, taste buds are located on the roof, sides and back of the mouth, and in the throat.

items.ok_line: Taste buds also sit in the mouth and throat.
items.ko_line: They are in the mouth and throat, not nose, lips, or stomach.
items.exp_text: Taste buds are not only on the tongue; others are found on the roof, sides and back of the mouth, and in the throat.

items.prompt: Which papillae on the tongue do NOT contain taste buds?

options.label: Filiform papillae
options.feedback: Correct. Filiform papillae are the exception—they do not contain taste buds, unlike the other papillae.

options.label: Fungiform papillae
options.feedback: Fungiform papillae do contain taste buds. The ones without them are the filiform papillae.

options.label: Circumvallate papillae
options.feedback: Circumvallate papillae contain taste buds. The exception is the filiform papillae.

options.label: Foliate papillae
options.feedback: Foliate papillae contain taste buds. The exception is the filiform papillae.

items.ok_line: Filiform papillae have no taste buds.
items.ko_line: It is filiform, not the others, that lack buds.
items.exp_text: Most papillae hold hundreds of taste buds, but filiform papillae are the exception: they contain no taste buds at all.
